title: Venture capital
note: What a founder needs to raise the odds of a paying exit: base rates, payout math, investor incentives, terms and the idea scorecard. Deal-term data is quarterly and tax law changes, so refresh every six months.

concepts.s: Three forces decide a VC-backed founder's payout: the power law that drives investors, the waterfall that decides who is paid first, and the option you keep by raising less.

x.b:
• Base rate: most VC-backed founders' equity ends at zero.
  • Power law: funds need rare giant exits, so they push every company toward one.
  • Waterfall: preferred stock is repaid before common, so money raised sets the exit price you need.
  • Optionality: bootstrap, raise small, or raise big; each changes the other two.

Your levers: sector and timing, investor experience, capital raised relative to a realistic exit, and the cost of each attempt.
Trap: Optimizing the headline valuation. It usually means a bigger preference stack and a higher exit price before common sees anything.
A $40M sale is life-changing with $8M raised and worth nothing to common with $45M raised.

cards.q: Same $40M exit, one company raised $8M and another $45M. Why do the founders' outcomes differ?
cards.a: Preferences: with $45M raised, investors take the whole sale before common gets anything.

cards.q: Why do VCs push for bigger outcomes than founders may want?
cards.a: Fund returns follow a power law, so only rare giant exits move the fund.

concepts.s: In the largest study, 84% of VC-backed founders got nothing at exit, and those paid had a median of about $5.6M, so plan around the median, not the mean.

x.b:
Azevedo, Scheuer, Smetters and Yang (NBER w34512, 2025): about 96,000 US startups, 1987-2021. 16% of founders had a positive payoff (mean about $45.6M, median about $5.6M after tax); the top 2% captured 80% of founder value. A revised draft (July 2026) is harsher: 88% zero, and the top 1% hold 79%.

Repeated tries: P(at least one) = 1 - (1 - p)^n. At p = 12%, four attempts give about 40%; expected attempts to one success is 1/p, roughly 6-8. Each takes years.

Trap: "An exit" is not a founder win. A sale can return nothing to common after preferences.
Trap: Assuming failure raises the next try's odds. It barely does (next concept).
At 15% per attempt, three attempts give about 39%. A decade of tries still leaves the majority with no paying exit.

cards.q: At a 12% per-attempt rate, what is the chance of at least one paying exit in 4 tries?
Among founders with any payoff in NBER w34512, why plan on the median instead of the mean?
cards.a: The mean (about $45.6M) is pulled up by a few outliers; the median is about $5.6M.

concepts.s: Prior success, the industry and year you start in, and, for first-time founders, an experienced VC are the best-documented predictors; a prior failure barely helps.

x.b:
Gompers, Kovner, Lerner and Scharfstein (2010), success meaning an IPO or filing: 30% for founders with a prior success, 18% for first-timers, 20% after a failure. The industry-year of the first venture predicted the next: 52% of 1983 computer startups went public versus 18% of 1985's. For first-time founders, the paper's model predicts 20.9% success with more experienced VCs versus 14.3% with less experienced ones.

Picking investors: firm experience, the partner's board record, back-channel references from founders whose companies failed, and follow-on behavior. Noise: brand alone, the top valuation.
Trap: "Failure teaches." In this data a failed founder is close to a fresh draw.
Two term sheets: a top valuation from a new fund, a lower one from a partner with ten board seats. For a first-time founder the data favors the second.

cards.q: A first-time founder chooses between a novice fund's higher valuation and an experienced firm. What does the evidence favor?
cards.a: The experienced firm: a predicted 20.9% vs 14.3% success for first-time founders.

cards.q: Which references reveal the most about an investor?
cards.a: Back-channel references from founders whose companies failed.

concepts.s: Preferred investors are repaid before common stock, so the total preference stack decides whether founders are paid in a modest exit.

x.b:
• 1x non-participating (standard): at exit the investor takes the greater of its money back or its as-converted share. Cooley's Q2 2026 data: about 96% of deals at 1x and 96% non-participating.
  • Participating: money back plus a share of the rest. Multiples (2x) and seniority push common further back.

Trap: Bridge rounds often add seniority or extra preference.
Synthesis: Keep total preferences well below a realistic exit price (say under a third). Rule of thumb, not research.

$40M raised at 1x non-participating for 50%. Sale at $50M: converting gives $25M, so investors take $40M; common splits $10M, and a founder with 20% of the company (40% of common) gets $4M. At $30M, common gets zero.

cards.q: $40M preference, 1x non-participating, investors own 50%, sale at $50M. What does common get?
cards.a: $10M: investors take the larger of $40M preference or $25M as-converted.

cards.q: Same stack, sale at $30M. What does common get?
cards.a: Zero; investors take all $30M.

cards.q: What is participating preferred?
cards.a: The investor takes its money back and then also shares pro rata in what remains.

concepts.s: Each priced round typically sells about a fifth of the company, and with SAFEs and option pools the median founding team holds about 56% after seed and 36% after Series A.

x.b:
Carta data: median dilution about 20% at seed and at Series A; median founding-team ownership about 56% after seed and 36% after Series A; under 10% of 2025 software seeds sold 30% or more.

  • Option pool shuffle: a pool created in the pre-money dilutes only existing holders, lowering the effective price.
  • SAFE (Y Combinator): not debt; converts at the next priced round at the better of cap or discount. A post-money SAFE fixes the holder's stake ($1M at a $10M cap = 10%), so all SAFE dilution falls on founders, then stacks with the round.
  • Convertible notes are debt with interest and a maturity date; at maturity, principal plus interest comes due unless it converts or is extended.
Trap: Reading ownership pre-pool. Always look at fully diluted ownership, including the pool and all convertibles.
Three post-money SAFEs at 10%, 8% and 7% mean founders give up about a quarter before the seed round takes its 20%.

cards.q: $1M post-money SAFE at a $10M cap: what does the holder own before the priced round's new money?
Why does an option pool set in the pre-money lower your effective valuation?
cards.a: Only existing holders are diluted by it, so the new investor's price per share effectively falls.

concepts.s: A venture fund needs a few companies to return the whole fund, so investors prefer a small chance at a huge exit while founders often prefer a high chance at a decent one.

x.b:
Horsley Bridge data shared with Andreessen Horowitz: about 6% of investments, using 4.5% of dollars, produced about 60% of returns; the best funds lost money on more deals, not fewer.

A $100M fund owning 10% needs a roughly $1B exit to return the fund once. Misalignment shows in early acquisition offers, pressure to raise more, and protective provisions that let preferred block a sale.
Trap: Discovering misalignment at the exit, after the veto rights are signed. Discuss exit expectations before taking money.
A $60M offer can change a founder's life and be irrelevant to a $500M fund. A small seed fund or angels may welcome that outcome; match fund size to your realistic exit.

cards.q: A $100M fund owns 10% of you at exit. How big must the exit be to return the fund?
cards.a: About $1B.

cards.q: How can a founder reduce pressure to reject a good early offer?
cards.a: Pick investors whose fund size fits a realistic exit, align on exits upfront, or take a secondary later.

concepts.s: Raise venture money only for a market that can produce a very large company fast; otherwise customers, savings, debt and grants keep both your ownership and your exit options.

x.b:
• Routes: bootstrapping, customer prepayment and paid pilots, angels and small funds, revenue-based financing (for recurring revenue), bank or SBA loans, non-dilutive SBIR/STTR awards, grants or contracts (reauthorized through Sept 30, 2031).
  • VC fits: a winner-take-most market and growth that needs capital before revenue can fund it.
  • Pay while you build: cost = (market pay - founder pay) x years + re-entry cost. Build beside your job before traction; go all-in when pay is within about 15% of market (the scorecard's rule, a judgment).

Trap: Raising because it signals success. Every round raises the exit price common needs.
Synthesis: The NBER and Gompers numbers describe only VC-backed companies; non-VC payoffs have a different, less extreme shape.
A $5M-a-year niche SaaS is a great bootstrapped business and a failed venture investment.

cards.q: Name a non-dilutive funding source for US R&D startups.
cards.a: SBIR/STTR awards (grants or contracts), authorized through September 30, 2031.

cards.q: When does the scorecard say to go all-in on a startup?
cards.a: When funding or revenue can pay you within about 15% of market.

concepts.n: Term sheet terms that move money and control
concepts.s: Beyond valuation, preference, participation, anti-dilution, dividends, pay-to-play and control rights decide who gets paid and who decides.

x.b:
• Anti-dilution: broad-based weighted average is standard; full ratchet (reset to the new lower price) is harsh.
  • Dividends: non-cumulative is standard; cumulative ones add to the preference.
  • Redemption: investors can force a buyback; rare and investor-friendly.
  • Pay-to-play: holdouts lose preferred rights; Cooley saw it in 8.4% of Q2 2026 deals.
  • Control: board seats, protective provisions (veto over a sale or senior stock), drag-along.

Trap: A high valuation with a full ratchet, participation or a 2x preference can cost more at exit than a lower clean round.
Trap: Losing the board early means losing the CEO seat and the sale decision.
Raising $5M: a clean round at $20M post leaves common $30M of a $40M exit; at $30M post with a 2x participating preference, common gets $25M.

cards.q: Which anti-dilution clause is standard, and which is harsh?
cards.a: Broad-based weighted average is standard; full ratchet is harsh.

cards.q: What do protective provisions let preferred holders do?
cards.a: Veto key actions such as selling the company or issuing senior stock.

concepts.s: Vest founders over four years with a one-year cliff, file the 83(b) within 30 days, and set up as a C corporation to keep QSBS available.

x.b:
• Acceleration: double-trigger (sale plus termination) is what acquirers accept; single-trigger vests on sale.
  • 83(b): pay tax on today's low value, not at each vesting date. The 30-day deadline cannot be extended.
  • QSBS (Section 1202), stock issued after July 4, 2025: 50% exclusion after 3 years, 75% after 4, 100% after 5; cap the greater of $15M or 10x basis; $75M gross-asset limit. Older stock: 5 years, $10M, $50M. Study material, not tax advice.

Trap: Missing the 83(b): tax arrives at each vesting date at the higher value, often with no cash to pay it.
Trap: LLC first, convert late: the QSBS clock starts only at C-corp stock issuance.
Sell QSBS stock (issued 2026) after 4 years for a $10M gain: 75% excluded; the rest is taxed at up to 28%, plus possibly the 3.8% net investment income tax.

cards.q: What QSBS exclusion applies after 4 years for stock issued after July 4, 2025?
You got restricted founder stock 40 days ago. What did you likely lose?
cards.a: The 83(b) election, which must be filed within 30 days.

concepts.s: Run four pass-or-fail gates before scoring an idea, then score survivors on six weighted criteria, knowing only two have research behind them.

x.b:
Gates: (1) exit path: three or more named acquirers and real deals; (2) common gets paid at a median exit after preferences; (3) work mode fits the stage; (4) kill criteria (milestone, metric, date) written first.

Scores (1-5): edge 25, sector base rate 20, distribution 20 (first 10 customers by name), iteration cost 15 (a test that could kill it in under 2 weeks), catalyst 10, investor fit 10. Sector timing and investor fit have research support; the rest is discipline.
Trap: Letting a high score rescue an idea that failed a gate. Gates are arithmetic; scores are not forecasts.
Strong edge and a named first 10 customers, but no plausible acquirers and $30M needed: it fails gate 1 or 2 regardless of score.

cards.q: An idea scores 4.4 but has no plausible acquirer. What does the scorecard say?
cards.a: Drop or restructure it: failing a gate overrides any score.

cards.q: Which two scored criteria have research behind them?
cards.a: Sector base rate (industry-year effect) and investor fit (experienced-VC effect).

concepts.s: Most founder payouts come from acquisitions, so cultivate acquirers early, keep the preference stack small, and model every term of an offer, not just the price.

x.b:
• Escrow and holdbacks: part of the price waits months for claims.
  • Earnouts: price tied to future targets, often after you lose control.
  • Retention packages: pay to key people outside the purchase price.
  • Management carve-outs: a slice for the team when preferences would leave common with nothing.

Run a competitive process when an offer arrives; one bidder sets the price.
Trap: Counting earnout money as yours. Many targets are never fully met.

$50M headline with $8M in escrow and a $12M earnout pays $30M at closing. With $20M of preferences paid first from the closing cash, common gets $10M at closing; the remaining $20M depends on escrow release and the earnout.

cards.q: $50M offer with an $8M escrow, a $12M earnout and $20M of preferences. What does common receive at closing?
cards.a: $10M: $30M is paid at close, and preferences take $20M of it first.

cards.q: What is a management carve-out?
cards.a: A slice of proceeds set aside for the team when preferences would leave common with little or nothing.
